name: Automotive Electronics
scope: ECU counts, CAN security, AEC qualification torture, tier-supplier structure

claims.claim_text: A large part of automotive silicon consists of small embedded microcontrollers doing airbag control and sensor signal conditioning, together with LIN and CAN transceivers and smart sensors, rather than high-performance processors.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're doing a lot of automotive parts. And they have little embedded microcontrollers that do things like airbag control and sensors, you know, signal conditioning on the sensor, basically. Lin bus, can bus kind of stuff. Yeah. Lin transceivers, can transceivers, smart sensor signal conditioning with a microcontroller on board
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Automotive-qualified vendors such as Infineon are largely invisible to engineers outside the sector: their parts are priced for automotive volumes and are not sold in low quantities, so a designer searching a catalogue distributor rarely reaches them.
claims.quote_verbatim: they might not use Infineon parts because they're automotive qualified. They make tons of parts, but most people outside automotive. They're expensive. You don't, can't afford them and yeah, and they don't do low quantity
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Worktrips and Workspaces - Junket Jactation Jiltedness

claims.claim_text: A modern car contains on the order of one hundred to three hundred microcontrollers, which is why automotive development leans on multi-node system simulation in the same way satellite work does.
claims.quote_verbatim: We have customers in automotive. Same story. In a car, you'll find like 100. 200, 300 micros in there
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Several semiconductor makers deliberately do not advance process nodes, serving automotive and medical customers from older equipment and 8-inch rather than 12-inch wafers, because those parts do not need billions of transistors and their customers value process continuity.
claims.quote_verbatim: a business model of not advancing to the newer technologies, but rather providing technologies for medical and automotive and, you know, parts that don't need to have billions of transistors. Yep. Right. Yeah, like stay on that old node, use the old equipment, stay on the 8-inch wafer instead of 12-inch
claims.speaker: Jake Baker
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: Automotive-grade electronics are qualified across roughly minus 40 to plus 125 degrees Celsius.
claims.quote_verbatim: Minus 40 is impressive to 125
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: Temperature qualification in a car depends on where the module sits: electronics in the passenger compartment are typically rated minus 40 to plus 85 degrees Celsius.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're just in the passenger compartment somewhere, typically you're minus 40 to plus 85C
claims.speaker: Speaker ?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Chips are graded into consumer, industrial, automotive and military temperature ranges, with industrial and automotive commonly sharing the minus 40 to plus 85 degree band.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is the consumer temperature grade. There's the automotive temperature grade. And there's the military temperature grade. You have industrial in there, too. Oh, industrial. Industrial, sorry. They're usually the same. And so, that's normally your minus 40 to plus 85
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: A module mounted against the metal roof, such as an overhead console, is rated to 105 degrees Celsius rather than 85, and the higher grade carries a price premium that keeps designers on the lower grade wherever they can stay there.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you're 105C. Yeah. Yeah. You know, that's what I think of it as automotive. I would think 85 is usually industrial and 105 is automotive because I never buy 105 because you have to pay more
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers frequently qualify an existing part up to 125 degrees rather than 85 and sell it under the same part number, which merges the automotive and industrial demand pools onto one item.
claims.quote_verbatim: qualified for auto processes these days. You know, they'll just be like, oh yeah, we qualify that up to 125 instead of 85
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: When an automotive and an industrial customer share a part number, allocation during a shortage follows volume, so a small buyer competing against a vehicle programme simply does not receive parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's either Chris Gammell buying 10s or the Ford F-150. God knows how many. A hundred million or something. Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And it's just like, there's just no way I'm going to, I'm going to get that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: Automotive-rated parts are sometimes cheaper than their non-automotive equivalents, because the volumes they are manufactured in outweigh the cost of the higher qualification.
claims.quote_verbatim: automotive rated products can be cheaper than the non-automotive. Oh, wait, really? Which is quite interesting. Yeah, because, well, because of the high volume they're manufactured in
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: An explicit ten-year supply guarantee in a part's headline features signals that the vendor is aiming it at industrial or automotive customers, for whom supply horizon is a selection criterion.
claims.quote_verbatim: 10 year supply guarantee. To me, that's always like, Hey, we are targeting industrial, right? Or we're targeting automotive
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shine A Light

claims.claim_text: Automakers require ten-year supply agreements, and a low-volume buyer who cannot promise large orders can still obtain such an agreement by offering the vendor a guaranteed long-term revenue stream instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: Automakers need 10 year agreements. Right. Yes. I think, I think, I think for low volume where you're not going to be able to show up with, you know, a million dollars at the door, you're not, you're not getting the foot massages. Right. Right. You're, you're a small time player, but you can guarantee this like longer term income
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: Automotive designs need peripheral counts that general-purpose microcontroller vendors do not offer, such as four LIN controllers and two CAN controllers on one device, which is one reason the sector concentrates on a small set of automotive-focused suppliers.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want four LIN controllers and two CAN controllers. And they're like, huh? We've got one part that has one CAN controller. Good luck. Right. Yeah. Yeah. That's it. And, and like all the, and the software certification is, is huge for those sorts of things. And they're just, you know, and the platform certifications and everything else in there. That's just what that industry uses
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A House of FR4

claims.claim_text: Software and platform certification are as large a factor as silicon in automotive part selection, which further narrows the field of usable vendors.
claims.quote_verbatim: the software certification is, is huge for those sorts of things. And they're just, you know, and the platform certifications
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A House of FR4

claims.claim_text: Automotive-focused semiconductor vendors cannot discontinue old 8-bit microcontrollers at will, because their largest customers have designed them into vehicles still in production.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can't just tell, you know, Ford and Toyota, no, piss off, we're not going to make the 8-bit micros anymore. They can at their own detriment, right, at their own peril
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Hardware has no partial-completion state: a single missing component stops a production line, which is why component shortages hit vehicle production directly rather than merely delaying features.
claims.quote_verbatim: every single part has to be right on the board. Yeah. Yeah. One part and you were lined down
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Toasted Marshmallow Connectors

claims.claim_text: Large automotive suppliers such as Continental established engineering sites in Romania because the local engineering talent is cheaper than in western Europe, and in some regions those firms are essentially the whole electronics job market.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the obvious choice for these big automotive companies like Continental and others to open up shop here in Romania because there are a lot of talented young people. And it's probably cheaper for them to hire talent here than it is in the west of Europe
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: Tier-one suppliers such as Continental and Bosch design the electronics that goes into vehicles from many different brands, so cars from Fiat, Peugeot and Renault can contain substantially the same electronic modules.
claims.quote_verbatim: our main clients was continental and Bosch. Mm-hmm . So yeah. And so basically, yeah, they do all these electronics, which goes inside different cars. So, you know, it doesn't matter then if you then buy a Fiat or a Peugeot or a Renault. Right. They, they, they have, you know, probably same parts, you know, at least for the electronics
claims.speaker: Andrea Longobardi
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: Because the tier-one supplier aggregates designs across many carmakers, it approaches semiconductor vendors with combined volume and negotiates as a very large customer, which is a structural advantage the individual carmakers do not have.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they approach a maximum or a TI or ST, they can be like, Hey, look, we've got all these designs. We're a really big customer as well
claims.speaker: Andrea Longobardi
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: For microcontroller vendors such as Renesas the automotive segment, not the hobbyist or maker segment, is where the revenue is, which shapes their product roadmaps and tool ecosystems.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of their big markets for their processors is not the sort of like the hobby kind of, you know, hacker markets that we're kind of into, right? It's in the automotive space. They're in the place where there's actually money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Altium...Acquired!

claims.claim_text: Automotive microcontroller share has long been concentrated in the ex-Motorola line that became Freescale and then NXP, a position built on the older MC series designed into vehicles.
claims.quote_verbatim: Freescale, because they're using all the automotive stuff, right? This is the old Motorola
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Small configurable mixed-signal parts find automotive use as single-purpose workaround devices: a carmaker needing one specific problem solved on a load-dump-capable board will design one in across a million units.
claims.quote_verbatim: someone doing like a load dump test capable board at a car manufacturer. And they're going to make a million of them. You know, Toyota is going to make a million of these things and they just need this one thing to work around this one problem they have. And it's going in there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: An automotive high-side switch is a MOSFET with added protection intelligence: it is driven by a simple logic level like any switch, but protects itself against transients, over-temperature and over-current without external circuitry.
claims.quote_verbatim: automotive high side switches are like, you know, a MOSFET, just that it has some added intelligence. It has some added protection features. So you deal with it approximately the same way. You just switch a logic high or low to control it, but it does its own thing to protect it, to protect it against transients, to protect it from over temperature, over current situations
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: A DC-DC converter feeding from a vehicle's 12 volt line must be automotive grade, because the transients present on that rail will eventually destroy an ordinary converter even though it works on the bench.
claims.quote_verbatim: it also contains an automotive grade DC to DC converter for power because, you know, you can't just go and use any DC to DC converter on one of these boards because what might happen is there are a lot of transients on the, like the 12 volt line on a typical car. So there is a high chance that typical converter might fail at some point due to all the stress that it encounters
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: During a cold crank the nominal 12 volt supply can collapse to around four volts while the starter turns the engine, so every module powered from that rail must survive and ideally continue operating through the dip.
claims.quote_verbatim: 12-volt batteries, they said those things will get down to, like, four volts, and they'll have to try and jump a car. Yeah. You know, like, try and crank a... Oh, I'm getting in trouble already. Try and turn over the engine, basically, with, you know, this battery. But it's usually 12, and now it's at four, and it's like, that's not gonna... That can ruin your day
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: An automotive ambient specification of 85 degrees is a starting point rather than a limit: the die temperature rise from the module's own dissipation sits on top of that ambient, which is what makes thermal simulation load-bearing in automotive design.
claims.quote_verbatim: this can work up to like, you know, 85 C no problem. So that means you have temp rise on top of 85 C
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Kreuzer

claims.claim_text: The wide automotive temperature range means every design engineer in the sector works fluently with junction-to-ambient thermal resistance and performs thermal analysis as routine practice, even on otherwise simple body electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: every design engineer has a very good working knowledge about, you know, R theta JA and, you know, how that all matters, you know, so, you know, to really know how to do that thermal analysis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Automotive modules are effectively powered for ten years, since a great deal of vehicle electronics remains energised with the key off, which makes quiescent current and long-term reliability first-order design parameters.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of these things, they really are, they really are powered for 10 years. Right. I mean, it's not like it's, you know, even though the key is off
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: The vehicle electrical architecture moved from a mechanical ignition switch carrying 40 amps that cut everything dead, to a permanently networked system of buses in which nothing is fully switched off.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ignition switch in your car was this 40 amp switch, right? Yeah. That's right. It just went cold, you know? And that ain't the case anymore. You know, there's, there's all sorts of stuff on and, you know, everything's all network together. There's, you know, all these buses and things
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Multi-layer ceramic capacitors have become thin enough that mechanical stress or a board flex fracture turns the part into a resistor rather than an open circuit, a leading failure mode in vibration-exposed equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: those multi-layer ceramic capacitors. Oh, yes. Because they're so thin now. The layers are so thin that the slightest stress or fracture turns them into a resistor
claims.speaker: Big Clive
claims.episode_title: The King of Trash with Big Clive

claims.claim_text: Flexible-termination MLCCs, whose end caps float on a compliant layer to absorb board stress, exist specifically for automotive and other high-vibration applications.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're designed for the automotive industry and high vibration industries. They're a multi-layer ceramic capacitor that the end caps on them that sold to the PCB, they're actually like, kind of like floating. They're kind of like wobbly. It's got this flexible end thing to take out the stress
claims.speaker: Big Clive
claims.episode_title: The King of Trash with Big Clive

claims.claim_text: A cracked ceramic capacitor presents as unexplained battery drain rather than as a functional fault; the usual culprit is the first ceramic across the battery, and the leakage is visible as a warm spot under a thermal camera.
claims.quote_verbatim: its quiescent current should be real low, but it's just eating the batteries. And the culprit is always the first little ceramic capacitor across the battery. Yeah. It's just basically just discharging it
claims.speaker: Big Clive
claims.episode_title: The King of Trash with Big Clive

claims.claim_text: Automotive-oriented parts often integrate drive capability that general-purpose logic lacks, such as a 595 shift register rated 250 milliamps per channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is an automotive part and it can drive a bunch of current per pin, 250 milliamps per channel
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Custodial Arts

claims.claim_text: The high-current automotive shift register is functionally a 595 shift register merged with a 2803 open-drain driver array, saving a package and the interconnect between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically combining a 595 with a 2803 driver. Is that basically it? A 2803 open drain driver
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Custodial Arts

claims.claim_text: Automotive EMC discipline began as self-imposed industry restriction rather than external regulation, driven by the consequences of interference in engine control, airbag and cruise control circuits.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want your cruise control to go crazy. That's it. So, you know, automotive has a lot of – it originally started out as self-imposed restrictions. It's just because of what the product is
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Vehicle control is conventionally split between the engine control unit, responsible for keeping engine performance within specification, and the body control unit, which handles door locks, windows, seats and other non-powertrain functions.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's, in a car, there's usually two main control units, you have the ECU, the engine control unit, that's responsible for making sure that the engine performance is within specifications, and then the BCU, the body control unit
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: The engine control unit is deliberately given no responsibility it does not need, and is built with multiple processors running in lockstep checking one another, because a fault that mistimes variable valve timing destroys the engine.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of times they have multiple processors in there that are all running in lockstep checking each other
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Warranty liability drives ECU robustness directly: with a hundred-thousand-mile engine warranty, an ECU fault that damages an engine at sixty thousand miles is a warranty replacement, so carmakers over-engineer the ECU against that specific exposure.
claims.quote_verbatim: a hundred thousand mile engine warranty. You don't want the ECU to blow your engine up at sixty thousand miles and they owe you a new one
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Sensors feeding the engine ECU are usually wired point to point rather than placed on the CAN bus, which limits the damage a bus fault or bus intruder can do to engine control.
claims.quote_verbatim: the engine ECU is in charge under the hood, it's, you know, reading all of those sensors and calculating the correct spark advance and things, basically everything is paying attention to the ECU, quite often the sensors are not connected via a can or anything, the ECU will have dedicated wires for that, so you can't really screw it up too badly
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Vehicle architectures differ in whether a single supervisor exists: in the Tesla Model S the computer behind the seventeen-inch centre display is the central brain and controls the drivetrain and ABS, whereas most cars distribute authority and give modules substantial autonomy.
claims.quote_verbatim: in a Tesla, you'd almost be right. The Tesla Model S, that big 17-inch center display has a computer back inside of it, and that computer is the central brain box of the whole car and really does control everything else. You know, the drivetrain is controlled by the center computer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Separate vehicle modules were consolidated into the body control module because integration reduces mass and wiring, which feeds directly into CAFE fuel economy, emissions and weight requirements.
claims.quote_verbatim: cafe and weight requirements and gasoline emissions and, you know, fuel efficiency
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: ECU silicon roadmaps are driven by margin: the supplier integrates as much as possible onto the chip to avoid populating external parts, which also reduces the number of separate devices the buyer must source during a shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: to do that for, uh, an engine control unit, you basically need to integrate. Integrate as much as possible into a chip and avoid populating that stuff as external on, on a PCB
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: A carmaker reported spending twenty to twenty-five percent of its research and development effort on the hardware and software of the vehicle rather than on the mechanical product.
claims.quote_verbatim: they spend 20, 25% of their R&D time just developing the hardware and software for the car
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: Sensor content per vehicle was projected to average around twelve cameras per car alongside radar for collision detection, all layered on top of an already complex conventional vehicle electrical system.
claims.quote_verbatim: 12 cameras per car is going to be average because of just- Wow. Right? I mean, that's a ton. Yeah. You know? And then, like, all the vision stuff, and then radar for collision detection
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: A car wiring harness is built as a single custom cable assembly carrying LIN, CAN and power together and snaked through the vehicle, and automotive designers treat custom cable assemblies as the default rather than as a last resort because the distances rule out board-to-board connections.
claims.quote_verbatim: if people want to really see or just look up car harnesses, that's like on the extreme end. Ah, ah, ah. Yeah, yeah. Because they'll have a single harness assembly. And it's got, you know, it's got the LIN bus and the CAN bus and all the stuff that's in there. Yeah. And power and whatever. But it's a single thing. And then they just snake that son of a bitch right through the center of the car
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Interconnectorama

claims.claim_text: Layered abstraction that helps in general computing hurts in automotive embedded work, because low-level behaviour propagates upward; generated code following such abstractions has been observed at four to five times the size of the application itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: for embedded systems, you need to know things because they bubble up from the bottom and really hit you. Right. So, so somebody has said, oh, do this. And I've looked at some of the code generated and it's amazingly huge overheads. Yeah. You're talking kind of four or five times the size of the application
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: CAN was designed by Bosch in the mid-1980s as a multiplexing scheme to replace the individual signal wires then run point to point for each sensor value, which were turning the car into a copper harness problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: running bundles and bundles and bundles of wires around. And pretty soon, the car becomes less made of steel and more made of copper. And it was just running out of control
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: CAN is a publish-subscribe broadcast bus: a node publishes its sensor values, every other node sees them, and subscribers act on the ones they need. There is no addressing of a recipient.
claims.quote_verbatim: CAN is what they call a publish-subscribe model. So you publish all your sensor values, and then subscribers pick up them if they want them and do something with them if they want to
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: CAN was developed by Bosch in 1985.
claims.quote_verbatim: developed by Bosch in 1985
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: CAN appeared in Bosch engine control units from around 1986, a year after the protocol was defined.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was used in engine control units from Bosch starting in about 86
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: CAN was mandated in cars only from 2009, so despite dating from the mid-1980s it can be relied on as universally present in vehicles only from that model year onward.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was mandated in cars only starting in 2009, so we're only going on nine years of cars definitely having CAN
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: CAN arbitration is a bit-by-bit state machine: every contending node transmits and simultaneously reads back, and any node that reads a value different from the one it sent has lost priority and backs off. After the identifier field, by default eleven bits, exactly one node remains and the rest switch to receiving.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone sends their first bit and you read it back. And if you read back something different to what you sent, you can't be the highest priority because the zero, the first person with a zero in their, in the, in the, in the current bit must be the higher than you. So you back off and wait until the next can frame starts
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: The Bosch team that produced CAN started from an RS-485 multi-drop scheme with an addressing protocol; that worked but cost too much CPU load, so the arbitration was moved into hardware, and that hardware became CAN.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were looking to do 485 multi-drop and addressing scheme. And then that's what they succeed in doing, but it turned out to be too much CPU load. Uh, so they've been into hardware and that, that became can
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: CAN puts arbitration into the physical layer, so unlike Ethernet it has no collisions and no collision-induced throughput collapse.
claims.quote_verbatim: built into the physical layer is arbitration. Um, oh, okay. So there's no collision. That's what I was getting at. Is that Ethernet has tons of collisions
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Every CAN node is required to take itself off the bus if it determines it is babbling, a fail-silent requirement built into the protocol rather than added by the system designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: every CAN node has to be able to shut itself off if it thinks it's babbling on the bus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: CAN provides atomic broadcast, a property not offered by other field buses: when the transmitting controller reports a frame as sent, every live node on the bus has received it correctly.
claims.quote_verbatim: can provides you that as far as I'm aware, no other field bus provides is atomic broadcast. So this means that when the sender is sent to can frame and it's marked in its can controller sent every single online device on the bus has received it correctly
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: CAN acknowledgement works in-frame: at least one receiving node must pull the acknowledgement bit dominant against the transmitter's recessive bit, which tells the sender that its frame was heard on the bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: called an acknowledgement field. And at least one device has to, uh, pull a zero down into that. So you transmit a one and somebody has to transmit a zero. And that says that you are on the bus effectively because someone can hear you
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Any CAN node that detects an error asserts an error frame of six dominant bits, a pattern the bit-stuffing rule makes impossible in normal traffic, so every controller on the bus recognises it, discards the frame and resynchronises before the sender retries.
claims.quote_verbatim: It asserts what's called an error frame. And that is a six zero bits on the bus. And what that does is that there's a, there's a protocol, a bit stuffing protocol in can, uh, that basically doesn't allow six bits of the same sign to appear, uh, in the normal frame
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Systems are routinely built on CAN without their designers knowing atomic broadcast is what makes them work. Those systems then break with obscure race conditions when they are migrated to a faster bus such as Ethernet, which does not provide the guarantee.
claims.quote_verbatim: they build it without knowing this and it works really, really well. And they're like, wow, that was nice. You know, great. And then they go and move it to some higher speed bus, like Ethan or something. And then it all starts to fall apart with really weird race conditions
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: A 500 kilobit CAN bus carries roughly 4,700 messages per second, which sets the ceiling on how much vehicle data can be published.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Can bus is able to send on 500 kilobit bus, you can send about 4,700 messages per second
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: CAN FD adds a flexible data rate: arbitration proceeds at the usual 250 or 500 kilobits, then the data phase switches up to as much as 8 megabits per second with larger payloads.
claims.quote_verbatim: A normal CAN runs at a single speed. So you'll hear a lot of times say 250 kilobit bus or a 500 kilobit bus for CAN. It's pretty standard. Okay. The CAN FD has flexible data rates. So it can start out sending at say 500 kilobits. And then when it starts transmitting actual data and not just metadata, it can kick up to 8 megabits per second. So it's far faster in the data portion and it supports a lot larger payloads
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: The practical driver for CAN FD is ECU reflashing, where an image of a couple of megabytes has to be pushed over the vehicle bus and the higher data-phase rate directly shortens service time.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to be used at any rate for ECU flashing in a car where the extra speed might be handy if you have to flash say a 2 megabyte ECU flash file, then you kind of appreciate the much faster speed
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: CAN is differential, but a single-wire CAN variant exists that uses one of the two differential lines and omits the other, trading noise immunity for copper.
claims.quote_verbatim: CAN is actually differential, there's a couple of different CAN standards, there is single-wire CAN, which is single-ended, and single-wire CAN is basically just one wire from the differential CAN, and you basically don't use the other wire, so it's the same basic thing, just with less wires
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Classical CAN tops out at about one megabit per second, which is slow by modern standards and is why faster automotive buses were introduced alongside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it pretty much tops, it tops out at about a megabit
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Before CAN prevailed in the mid-2000s the SAE automotive bus standard was an umbrella over incompatible Ford, GM and Chrysler protocols that shared only a data rate, so it standardised almost nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a one that was standardized under the, the SAE, the Society of Automotive Engineers. And it was really a, it was really a mess. Because it, because basically it wasn't a standard. It was, it was kind of this umbrella thing that sat over the Ford way and the GM way and the Chrysler way. And they're all totally different, but they all had the same speed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: CAN displaced the manufacturer-specific automotive buses because chip vendors supported it, while the Ford, GM and Chrysler protocols each required a licensed standalone bus interface chip carrying both the physical layer and the MAC, which was expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: it had a tremendous amount of traction behind it in terms of the, the components that you could buy from the chip makers that supported CAN
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: A typical vehicle runs a high-speed one-megabit powertrain CAN carrying the engine and transmission controllers, with the instrument cluster acting as the gateway onto the other buses.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got a high speed CAN, that's your one megabit and that's your powertrain bus. And so on, so on there, you've got your transmission controller, you've got your engine controller. They live on that. And then like, they'll usually connect up to like your instrument cluster and that's, and that acts as a gateway
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: LIN exists as a cheap UART-based sub-bus so that low-importance modules can be moved off the CAN bus, keeping the number of CAN nodes low while many LIN sub-buses hang beneath it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you really remove the number of clients that are on the can bus, you know, so that number is really not super high. And then you, then you kind of put your sub modules on these, on these independent sub buses
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: LIN is cheaper than CAN because it runs on the UART peripheral of any microcontroller with no dedicated controller, and uses a single wire instead of a differential pair.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's mostly cheaper because you can, can run it on a UR peripheral of any microcontroller and only uses one wire, which is half the cost of two wires
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: CAN transceivers contain protective logic, typically a dominant-state timeout, so that a hung microcontroller cannot hold the bus dominant and take the whole network down.
claims.quote_verbatim: make sure that if your microcontroller gets stuck, that it doesn't allow you to drive the line dominant for long periods
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: CAN priority arbitration has a starvation failure mode: a node with a low identifier that transmits too frequently wins every arbitration and squeezes the other nodes off the bus, so message rates and identifier assignment have to be budgeted at design time rather than chosen per node.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got one sensor who's sending data every millisecond or however quick you've got the CAN set up, if you don't give enough time for other, uh, nodes to talk, then you can quite easily, uh, stop or you can quite easily kind of, uh, essentially span the network enough so that you can't read from other sensors
claims.speaker: Ronald Sousa
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ronald Sousa of Hash Define Electronics

claims.claim_text: One workable CAN scheduling pattern is a broadcast poll at a fixed interval, for example every 500 milliseconds, with all nodes required to answer inside that window before the next poll.
claims.quote_verbatim: every 500 milliseconds, I would sample the network. And so any data that I want to read from all of them, they should be able to come back and send their information within 500 milliseconds before I do the broadcast again
claims.speaker: Ronald Sousa
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ronald Sousa of Hash Define Electronics

claims.claim_text: Setting every node to transmit on the same exact period is a design error on CAN: the timers coincide, the lowest identifier wins every time, and the remaining nodes back off and drop their data indefinitely. Either stagger the periods or let the controller hardware handle retransmission.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I'm, if they're all being set up to send data once a second, because I, I stupidly, uh, wrote the code so that it will, it will, it will be basically every second, precisely every second, it will be, there'll be an interrupt asking for the data to be sent. You basically had like one sense of talking all the time and the rest kind of going, I can't talk right now. We'll, we'll just leave it
claims.speaker: Ronald Sousa
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ronald Sousa of Hash Define Electronics

claims.claim_text: Add-on equipment on a commercial vehicle normally runs its own CAN network rather than joining the vehicle's bus; the vehicle bus is joined only when a customer explicitly requires data from it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't often tend to connect your CAN system onto, uh, the truck CAN system, for example, you would, you, you, you only do that if you had to
claims.speaker: Ronald Sousa
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ronald Sousa of Hash Define Electronics

claims.claim_text: CAN message semantics are not standardised: identifiers, message contents and whether transmission is periodic or event-driven are established by whoever designs that particular network, and there is no lookup table that assigns a fixed identifier to a function.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has to be kind of established when, you know, by the people who are designing that canvas network, you know, these are the IDs, you know, we're going to do, let's say this style of messaging, it's going to go out on a fixed, like beat pulse or frequency, or this is going to be event driven
claims.speaker: Dean Pick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dean Pick

claims.claim_text: A CAN module cannot simply be added to an existing vehicle network and expected to work; either the existing devices must be configured to supply the information the new module needs or the new module must supply what they expect, which is why aftermarket suppliers work through the vehicle manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just drop, drop in a canvas module into the, into the bus and expect everything to work. It's, you know, these devices have to be set up to either provide the information we need, or we need to send the information they need in order for these, these features and functions to actually be, um, be working and useful for the writer
claims.speaker: Dean Pick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dean Pick

claims.claim_text: There is little standardisation between vehicle manufacturers in how CAN networks are used or routed; each does it its own way, and manufacturers have no commercial incentive to converge because the difficulty of interpreting their data is itself worth something to them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't necessarily say that any one that, you know, that Ford is going to do things the same way the GM does. They just don't. There's different ways of doing things, different ways of routing the buses between every manufacturer
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Carmakers change CAN communications between model years and between models, so a third-party product must be supported per vehicle variant rather than per protocol, which is a severe burden for a small supplier.
claims.quote_verbatim: the car companies feel free to switch that between model years, between models of cars
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Engine swaps between manufacturers, once feasible because the engine was electrically self-contained, are now blocked by the bus: the ECU expects messages from modules such as ABS or traction control that limit torque, and those messages differ between makers.
claims.quote_verbatim: it might be looking for a message from the ABS or traction control module so that if the traction control module detects that you're slipping, it tells the ECU to not let you have any more torque than a certain limit. So that you quit slipping. So it's always looking for messages. Now that makes it really tough to put, say, a Ford motor into a Chrysler because all the messages are different
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Sniffing a vehicle CAN bus yields every frame on it but no meaning, because each manufacturer keeps its own message definitions private; interpreting the traffic is a reverse-engineering exercise per vehicle.
claims.quote_verbatim: knowing what every byte of data means, that's a whole nother story because there is literally almost no standard. I mean, each manufacturer does have its own standards, but they're kind of secret about it and not releasing it to the public. So you kind of do a lot of reverse engineering to figure out what's going on on the bus and what each frame ID points to
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: When a manufacturer needs to send more data than a CAN frame holds, it splits the payload across several frames under its own protocol layered on top of CAN, which makes reverse-engineering that data substantially harder.
claims.quote_verbatim: they sometimes split their data across multiple CAN transmissions and they kind of add their own protocol on top of CAN bus to be able to reconstruct al
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: Putting an oscilloscope on a vehicle diagnostic port shows only a digital bit stream; the data is framed and encoded, so protocol decoding rather than analogue measurement is the only route to interpreting it.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you put a, an oscilloscope on that, all you're going to see is, you know, uh, ones and zeros basically, just, uh, digital signal that looks like nonsense
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Vehicles carry several physical layers besides CAN, including K-Line, L-Line, LIN and the older J1850; the legacy standards are largely gone but LIN remains widespread.
claims.quote_verbatim: K-Line, L-Line, Lin, and, um, you know, some of the old J-250 that sort of stuff. I've never heard those before. K-Line, L-Line? I mean, yeah, they're just, uh, there are other protocols, you know, you're frequently finding in cars. Some of them are not really being used anymore
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: FlexRay is a competing automotive bus running around 10 megabits per second, approaching Ethernet rates.
claims.quote_verbatim: FlexRay is a lot faster. I think 10 megabits per second
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Autonomous sensing exceeds what CAN can carry, so LIDAR and comparable sensors have pushed vehicles onto FlexRay and automotive Ethernet for the data path.
claims.quote_verbatim: the autonomous system is sending so much data so rapidly, you couldn't do that over a standard CAN bus where you have 50 kilobytes per second of transfer speed. So they're going to things like FlexRay and ethernet. And that's where you're seeing the autonomous systems. So there is kind of a transition in that respect to newer, faster buses that can handle the kind of load
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: A LIDAR sensor may update object distances a thousand to ten thousand times per second, and video-based autonomy cannot be carried over a CAN link at all, which sets the bandwidth requirement for the sensor bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: it could be updating the distance to objects a thousand times per second or 10,000 times per second
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Camera, LIDAR and other high-bandwidth subsystems keep their command and control on CAN while carrying the sensor data itself on a separate bus, so the control plane and the data plane are physically distinct.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're connected to CAN bus for command and control kind of, but they have a separate bus too for audiovisual things or in an autonomous system, a separate bus for the actual flow of video data or LIDAR data, but they still have command and control probably over CAN where there's still something, say the ECU is still telling the LIDAR sensor that what it wants to see
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: The internal vehicle network has essentially no security controls: CAN is a simple protocol with no authentication, so physical access to the bus wires confers control.
claims.quote_verbatim: the internal network is so wide open or so lacking in security controls because, I don't know if you've ever looked at CAN bus, but it's just a dead simple protocol. It's not much different than like a spy bus. You tug at a line and then you're in control. If you've got physical access to that line, bam, you're in
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Once an attacker controls any one device on a vehicle bus, moving to control of many others generally requires little further work, because the network is either flat or split into a few loosely isolated flat networks.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't take much to go from a foothold or control of one device on that CAN bus to gaining access or control over many devices on that CAN bus
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Every one of the hundreds of microcontrollers in a car is an attack surface, including peripheral devices such as a tyre sensor, because compromising any bus-connected module yields bus access.
claims.quote_verbatim: There are hundreds and hundreds of micros in a modern car. Yep. So, you can go through any one of them. You know, the flat tyre sensor has a micro in it, you know, and it hooks onto the bus and it reports back. Right? All you've got to do is, you know, put a wheel on there that has that low, you know, that has a hacked sensor in it, you know, and bingo, it's got access to the bus
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Tyre pressure monitors do not offer a path to arbitrary bus control because their transmissions are a fixed, very short packet format rather than complete CAN frames, and the receiver is correspondingly simple. Had they transmitted full CAN frames the exposure would have been severe.
claims.quote_verbatim: the packet format of these tire pressure monitors is very fixed and it's like a fixed number of bytes and it's a very small number of bytes and there isn't much there. It's not like the tire pressure monitor is transmitting a complete CAN bus packet, for example. So if the tire pressure monitor were transmitting a complete CAN bus packet, then that would be a huge avenue of attack
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Cars segment their CAN buses to keep critical systems away from user-accessible ones, but a gateway that speaks on both buses must always exist. In the Jeep case the attacker compromised the radio and used its access to hop across the gateway onto the critical bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: to some extent they try to segment them away. So the important stuff is not usually user accessible, but there's always going to have to be a gateway system somewhere that can talk on both buses at the same time
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Vehicle security research first demonstrated total control of a car through physical access to the CAN bus. Because that result depended on physical access, the same work was redone as a remote attack over the internet, and it was the remote version that established the exposure as a real one for shipped vehicles.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of people kind of poo-pooed that research and said, well, big deal. You had physical access. That's not that exciting. We don't really care about that. And so what they did was they kind of said, well, let's go back to the drawing board and figure out how we can demonstrate the same thing, but with a remote attack where we're anywhere over the internet and we can attack a car
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Automotive security decisions have a long latency: the architecture debate over whether to air-gap the vehicle bus from internet-connected systems happened roughly a decade before the vulnerable cars were being exploited, because the cars being attacked were designed about five years before they shipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: this debate was happening, you know, internal to the automakers probably 10 years ago. Right. And the cars that are getting exploited today are ones that have already shipped and were designed at least five years ago
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Safety-critical CAN messages such as steering position typically carry one or two extra bytes computed from the message contents, but manufacturers deliberately avoid standard CRC-5 or CRC-8 and use obscure proprietary encodings instead, so the check is a weak barrier to reproduction rather than an integrity standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't use, you know, like CRC five or CRC eight or anything, uh, that you could easily do yourself. They'll use some, they'll, they'll try to come up with as, as sneaky of a encoding scheme as possible for those security bytes
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Carmakers pair theft-prone assemblies such as engines and transmissions to the vehicle with a challenge-response exchange at startup; if the transmission cannot answer the ECU's challenge, the ECU will not let it engage a gear.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will have kind of like a, a startup sequence where when the transmission starts up and you go to start the car, the ECU. Right. It sounds like a challenge or something like challenge response. Yeah. Right. The, the ECU will send a challenge and if the transmission can't send the correct response back, the ECU will never ask it to go into gear
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Component pairing has a direct repair cost: a vehicle rebuilder must have the original airbag rebuilt rather than fit a replacement, because the car will not recognise a unit it did not come with.
claims.quote_verbatim: he rebuilds cars and he has to actually find someone to rebuild the original airbag because he hasn't been able to figure out how to, you know, make, um, how to get the car to recognize, you know, the, uh, the one it didn't come with
claims.speaker: Collin Kidder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: Newer vehicles require modules to authenticate to the ECU with encrypted keys before they are allowed to communicate on the bus, specifically to defeat installation of parts harvested from another car.
claims.quote_verbatim: modules will first try to authenticate with the ECU to make sure that they belong to that car. And they have not been like harvested from another car and just installed on this car. So they use some encrypted keys to authenticate. And only after authentication is successful, they start talking on the canvas
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: Vehicle modules cannot be removed and reprogrammed through a JTAG header in service, so every module carries a bootloader that validates the application at boot and can accept a replacement image over the vehicle network.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got all these different microcontrollers throughout a vehicle. And let's say somebody discovers a bug in the firmware of one of them. Oh, yeah. You can't really pull those things out of the car and open them up, plug into the JTAG header, and reprogram them
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers are progressively gatewaying and locking down the OBD-II port, which pushes third-party diagnostic products toward tapping the bus directly under the hood instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: gateways and things like that are making the OBD-II port, you know, increasingly locked down, so people are having to, you know, find other ways in
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Earl Sharpe and Collin Kidder

claims.claim_text: A commercial CAN injection theft tool was built into a JBL Bluetooth speaker so that possession of it is not incriminating, with the apparent USB cable actually a twisted-pair CAN connection. Internally it is about ten dollars of parts, a PIC18F with an on-chip CAN controller and transceiver, potted in resin to stop it being copied.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about $10 worth of electronics inside. So that's quite a markup from selling that. So it's a PIC-18F with an on-chip CAN controller and a CAN transceiver
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Headlights are now CAN-connected modules containing microcontrollers rather than simple bulbs, which is what makes the headlight housing a viable physical entry point to the vehicle bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: the headlights are all. Can devices now. Right. They used to just be. Can devices. Yeah. They used to just be like. A light bulb. But now it's got all these crazy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Engineering Optimization

claims.claim_text: The OBD connector originated in Californian clean-air actions as a standardised engine diagnostic interface with a standard connector and pinout, deliberately placed where it is accessible but not obtrusive.
claims.quote_verbatim: that OBD, that onboard diagnostics. And that was, uh, that was sort of, uh, started by, uh, California, uh, a long time ago, right? When they, that was part of their clean air
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Electrically the OBD port is nothing more than an access point onto the vehicle's CAN bus, which is why it is both the standard diagnostic entry and a standing security exposure.
claims.quote_verbatim: all that is, is it's just where the can bus goes to
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Because OBD-II is standardised, third-party tools connect through it to reprogram the engine control module, remapping fuel tables, boost pressure and spark timing, though such tools exist mainly for vehicles with a modification community.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are tools that connect to your CAN bus and your car with the OBD2 connector. And then you can actually kind of reprogram the main engine control module. So remap the fuel tables, change, you know, boost pressures if it's a turbocharged car, mess with spark timings, all that kind of good stuff
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Vehicle software updates delivered through the OBD port over a half-megabit CAN link are slow enough to dominate service time: four updates took four hours at the dealer.
claims.quote_verbatim: just to get some bloody software updates that chug through a half megabit can bus through the OBD thing. It takes my four hours to do four software updates
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Because CAN replaced per-switch wiring with a message whose bits map to individual devices, a vehicle's electrical validation is done by decoding messages, and a specific function such as a door lock can be verified by scoping the relevant bit position while operating the switch.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually see like if the door is, is locked and you know, at this bit position, cause it was a bit message that it should be a one. Then if you put the scope on it, you, and if you press the switch, you'll see that one at that particular bit position
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Reusing a vehicle's existing instrument cluster after a conversion is done by capturing bus traffic, identifying which message carries the gauge value, and then transmitting that identifier with the desired value.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just simply tap into the CAN bus, look at the data going by, you capture it, and you decode it. And you say, oh, that value is the gas gauge. And then I can then drive it with that same address and put the gas gauge needle to where I want
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: An electric drivetrain can be built with CAN as the only signal interconnect: battery packs daisy chain through small latching four-wire CAN connectors, heavy cables carry power only, and the charger and each inverter are addressed the same way from a central vehicle controller.
claims.quote_verbatim: the battery packs, they have a little four-wire, a nice little latching CAN bus connector in and out if you're daisy chaining them up. You know, there's an in and out. And then big fat wires that come off them deliver power to the drive system, but otherwise no other wires going in or out of those things
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: In a production electric drive system the power electronics account for about 2 percent loss and the motor about 5 to 5.5 percent across the bulk of the operating range.
claims.quote_verbatim: we only have 2% loss in our electronics in the drive system. So really, you know, the motor itself, its loss is about 5%, maybe 5.5% in the bulk of the operating range
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Regenerative braking is not a separate mechanism: torque in either direction is a sign change in software, and what the CAN bus carries to the inverter is simply a torque magnitude and direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: torque either direction is really just a minus sign on software. Nice. Either torque is in or out. It's one and the same. Make it sound so simple. At the high level, it is. It's that simple. You know, how much torque do you want? Which direction do you want it? I mean, that's really what the CAN bus delivers to an inverter
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Concentrating a module's interfaces onto CAN pays off beyond communication: every additional IO needs protection, board area, connector pins and its own test coverage, whereas a CAN-only module can be fully exercised with a CAN dongle and a programmable power supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's really nice to keep the amount of IOs to, to as little as possible because all of those need protection and they need to be tested and just more board space, more connector pins. So we really try to, you know, really limit everything to, to the canvas and then use that for everything. And it also means that in terms of test equipment, you really just need a can dongle
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: A CAN-based distributed architecture has no single point of failure in the communication path: with the radio acting as a dumb packet router, the battery and other modules remain reachable even if the onboard computer dies.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if our onboard computer dies, we could still talk to the battery module or talk to something else because it's just a dumb router that, that forwards packets back and forth to the shared canvas
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: A standard bus interface lets hardware and software development be decoupled: a module such as a door handle can be exercised from a laptop over a USB LIN dongle and handed off complete to whoever writes the body controller software.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just added hooked up to a USB Lin dongle and send commands from my, from my laptop and read back status. And when that is working, then you hand that off to the person that is doing the software of the body controller
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Airbag deployment does not depend on the bus: the squib fires autonomously and the airbag still works if the CAN interface fails, with the bus used only for status reporting and warning lamps.
claims.quote_verbatim: the squib, that's the propeller, that's the charge and, you know, that, that's not sitting on the can bus. Oh, no, no. That would be a, that works autonomously. Even if the can bus interface fails, right? The airbag would still work
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: DC fast charging hardware is trivial, amounting to two large pins and a contactor connected straight across the battery; the entire difficulty of the standards lies in the communication protocol.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fast charge DC charge standard, basically all it is, is two big pins in the socket and a contactor that connects straight across the battery. That's all it is. Um, the problem is the protocol
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: CHAdeMO is a simple, well-designed charging standard: it runs over CAN, assigns dedicated pins to dedicated functions and already supports exporting power from the vehicle for vehicle-to-grid use, but it requires separate AC and DC connectors.
claims.quote_verbatim: the nice thing about Chadimo is a really well-designed standard in, in it's simple. It uses canvas. It's got dedicated pins for dedicated functions and it already supports outputting power from the car. And there are actually some V2G trials, vehicle to grid trials going on in the UK at the moment with the Nissan Leaf. But unfortunately, the one downside of Chadimo uses separate connectors for AC and DC
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: CCS carries its charging dialogue over HomePlug Green PHY, a protocol originally designed for domestic powerline networking, apparently chosen because the application involves power rather than because the requirement called for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses a protocol called, uh, green fire, which was originally designed for power line communication, like domestic, you know, putting data over your main power lines. So someone obviously thought, okay, this is a power application. This is a power line protocol. Let's use that
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The entire information requirement of DC fast charging is the car telling the charger a current and a voltage. CHAdeMO does this over CAN; CCS does the same job over a heavily modulated, encrypted powerline protocol.
claims.quote_verbatim: all this thing needs to do is the car to tell the charger, give me 200 amps, this much voltage, give me a hundred amps of this mass voltage. And that's pretty much it. It's a very simple, you know, say Chadimo does it using, using can bus. It's really simple, but this green fire protocol has got, you know, ridiculous modulation
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: CAN is deceptively complex to implement in software: it looks like a shift register but the full protocol flow chart has many distinct paths, which is why bit-banged CAN implementations on programmable IO are notable achievements rather than routine.
claims.quote_verbatim: CAN is kind of a fiddly, it's kind of like SQL C where you think it's just a shift register. And actually there's, if you draw out the whole flow chart, there are lots of different paths through it. And getting all that running on a bit bang system is actually quite impressive
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: CAN is not confined to cars: it turns up in essentially any mobile system combining motor control with a battery, including humanoid robots.
claims.quote_verbatim: anything that has like a motor controller and a battery system as well. It's probably going to have a CAN bus
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Noisy Rude Bus

claims.claim_text: A modern motorcycle carries a full CAN-connected module suite in which the ECU handling fuelling and ignition talks to a fly-by-wire throttle, an ABS module and an active suspension module, matching car architecture in a far smaller package envelope.
claims.quote_verbatim: a modern, uh, motorcycle has a, has a whole suite of typically can bus connected modules. Uh, so you could have an ECU, which is doing the, uh, the fueling and the ignition. Well, it's talking to a, a fly by wire throttle device, which is controlling, you know, the throttle or the amount of air that's going into the engine, uh, which is talking to an ABS module, which is controlling the, the anti-lock brake system
claims.speaker: Dean Pick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dean Pick

claims.claim_text: A six-axis inertial measurement unit shared over the CAN bus gives every module lean angle, gradient, acceleration and slip state, which is what allows the vehicle's responses to rider input to be modified in context.
claims.quote_verbatim: It essentially gives these different, uh, CAN bus enabled devices, uh, an insight into exactly what the motorcycle is doing, how far it's leaned over, if it's going up or down a hill, how it's accelerating, if it's skidding, sliding, wheeling, um, just a really amazing window
claims.speaker: Dean Pick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dean Pick
